summary: Earth Analog Finder (Project Mirror World) is a mission-first discovery engine that searches the whole planet for terrestrial environments that can help us prepare for the Moon and Mars. Instead of looking up a short list of famous analog sites such as Antarctica or the Atacama, it starts from a planetary science question, translates it into measurable, physics-derived Earth requirements, and searches Earth observation data at global, regional, local and feature scales to surface candidates nobody has listed. A separate physics layer then evaluates each candidate, with uncertainty and sensitivity analysis, and states where the analogy breaks down (gravity, atmosphere, vacuum, radiation). An interactive map shows which areas were searched, which lacked data, and the evidence behind each candidate. This matters because looking alike is not the same as working alike. Mission planners, instrument teams and scientists need defensible, transparent analogs, not just similar-looking landscapes.
details:
What it does: Earth Analog Finder takes a user from a planetary question to an evaluated Earth site through six integrated modules: (1) Planetary targets turn a Moon or Mars research question into a sourced, machine-readable target profile. (2) Earth data is a pipeline for satellite imagery, elevation, geology and environmental datasets, with tiling and coverage tracking. (3) Discovery ML uses multiscale feature detection, segmentation and novelty detection to generate candidate locations, including ones never listed as analogs. (4) Physics validation tests each candidate with process-specific models plus sensitivity and Monte Carlo analysis. (5) Map and globe let users explore search coverage and candidates from global to feature scale. (6) The application ties everything into one guided user journey.


How it works: The engine proposes candidates and the physics layer decides whether they are defensible. For example, a river channel's bed shear stress (τb = ρf·g·R·S) depends on gravity, so an Earth river must be interpreted for Mars rather than copied. Every candidate comes with its evidence, uncertainty, missing data and where the analogy breaks down.
Benefits and impact: Mission planners can choose and rehearse landing and base sites. Robotics and instrument teams can test technology in the right terrain. Planetary scientists can find overlooked places to study processes. Educators can show how Earth prepares us for new worlds.


Creativity: It is a search, not a lookup. It separates morphological resemblance, geological similarity, physical-process similarity and scientific usefulness. It records which areas were searched, unsearched, low-confidence or without data, so it never claims coverage it has not achieved.


Tools and data: Python, PyTorch/TensorFlow, geospatial tools, a JavaScript/React frontend with a web map library. Data sources: NASA Earthdata Search (https://search.earthdata.nasa.gov/), Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/), ESA Open Science Data (https://opensciencedata.esa.int/).
Factors considered: Equifinality (similar forms can come from different processes), differences in gravity and atmosphere, data uncertainty, and keeping "implemented," "tested" and "scientifically validated" claims separate.
